# Modern Web Guidance [Modern Web Guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. *Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.* [Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) ## Quickstart ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install ``` This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below. #### Try it out (without installing) ```shell # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . ``` ## Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. **Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: * **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. * **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. ## What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. ### Core Disciplines

🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ [the `navigation-drawer` guide](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md). #### The full list

**[identify-heavy-scripts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/identify-heavy-scripts.md)**: Identify the scripts most responsible for long animation frames - **[identify-inp-causes](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/identify-inp-causes.md)**: Identify slow-running JavaScript and other causes of poor Interaction to Next Paint (INP) responsiveness. - **[improve-next-page-load-performance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/improve-next-page-load-performance.md)**: Improve page load performance by prefetching or prerendering pages that the user is likely to visit next. - **[interaction-paint-timing](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/interaction-paint-timing.md)**: Measure the time it takes for user interactions and client-side navigations to render new contentful updates on screen. - **[interactions-in-complex-layouts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/interactions-in-complex-layouts.md)**: Make interactions snappier and more responsive (reducing Interaction to Next Paint (INP) scores) by avoiding layout re-calculations in complex layouts, such as data-heavy dashboards or spreadsheet-style grids. - **[lazy-load-video-and-audio](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/lazy-load-video-and-audio.md)**: Defer downloading offscreen video and audio assets, including video poster images and preloaded media data, until the media player approaches the viewport to conserve bandwidth and reduce network contention during initial page load. - **[optimize-image-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-image-priority.md)**: Optimize the loading priority of Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) candidate images and deprioritize non-critical images to reduce critical resource load delays. - **[optimize-preload-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-preload-priority.md)**: Optimize the relative priority of preloaded content to reduce critical resource load delays. - **[optimize-script-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-script-priority.md)**: Optimize the loading priority of scripts by boosting critical asynchronous scripts and deprioritizing non-essential or late-body scripts to improve sequencing and reduce delays. - **[out-of-order-html-streaming](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/out-of-order-html-streaming.md)**: Declaratively update a page with content streamed later into the same HTML document or via imperative JavaScript APIs. - **[resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.md)**: Use resolution-optimized images in CSS pseudo-elements (such as `::before` and `::after`) to reduce the number of DOM nodes. - **[schedule-tasks-by-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/schedule-tasks-by-priority.md)**: Schedule, reprioritize, or abort queued tasks across priority levels so critical user input runs ahead of background work.

privacy

- **[privacy](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/privacy/privacy.md)**: Action-oriented guidelines for web developers to implement privacy by design, data minimization, third-party audits, and secure data handling. Use this skill when designing applications, integrating third-party services, handling user data, or configuring security headers.

pwa

- **[install-web-app](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/pwa/install-web-app.md)**: Install web applications from a page using browser-controlled consent UI. - **[migrate-web-app-origin](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/pwa/migrate-web-app-origin.md)**: Transfer an installed web app to a new origin while preserving user configuration and OS-level shortcuts.

security

- **[client-side-encryption](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/client-side-encryption.md)**: Establish shared secrets using public-key encapsulation or key agreement—including hybrid and post-quantum protection—and encrypt sensitive data in the browser with authenticated encryption. - **[digital-signatures](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/digital-signatures.md)**: Sign and verify messages, tokens, or artifacts in the browser using classical or quantum-resistant (post-quantum) asymmetric keys to ensure data integrity and authenticity. - **[local-network-access](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/local-network-access.md)**: Access resources on a user's local network or loopback interface from a public web application. - **[passkey-authentication](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/passkey-authentication.md)**: Authenticate a returning user with a passkey for primary sign-in. - **[passkey-conditional-create](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/passkey-conditional-create.md)**: Silently register a passkey for an existing user after a successful password login. - **[passkey-management](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/passkey-management.md)**: Let users view and manage the passkeys registered to their account. - **[passkey-reauthentication](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/passkey-reauthentication.md)**: Verify a signed-in user's identity using their existing passkeys before a sensitive action. - **[passkey-registration](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/passkey-registration.md)**: Register a passkey for an existing user account. - **[passkeys](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/passkeys.md)**: Comprehensive orientation and cross-cutting principles for implementing WebAuthn and Passkeys in web applications. Use this guide when handling passkey registration, authentication, management, or reauthentication. - **[quick-sign-ins](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/quick-sign-ins.md)**: Authenticate returning users in place with their saved passkeys or passwords before navigating to a sign-in page or interrupting their workflow. - **[restrict-outbound-connections](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/restrict-outbound-connections.md)**: Restrict a page or worker to communicating only with an explicit allowlist of network endpoints to prevent unauthorized third-party requests and client-side data exfiltration. - **[sanitize-untrusted-html](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/sanitize-untrusted-html.md)**: Safely parse and display untrusted HTML content from user input by removing unsafe elements and attributes. - **[secure-external-subresources](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/secure-external-subresources.md)**: Verify the cryptographic integrity of external scripts, stylesheets, fonts, and images loaded from third-party origins, and control whether those requests send credentials or referrer URLs. - **[trusted-types](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/trusted-types.md)**: Prevent DOM-based XSS attacks by defining a Trusted Types policy to sanitize untrusted HTML, using the policy when writing to DOM sinks like innerHTML, and enforcing Trusted Types via Content Security Policy. - **[validate-origins](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/validate-origins.md)**: Compare and validate web origins and sites safely across cross-document messages and URLs without error-prone string parsing. - **[verify-email-ownership](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/security/verify-email-ownership.md)**: Verify that a user owns an email address during account creation, sign-in, or recovery without sending a one-time passcode or magic link email.

ui-atoms

- **[carousel-slide-effects](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/carousel-slide-effects.md)**: Create a carousel of slides with images or other visual elements, where each slide animates as they enter/center/exit their scroller. For example, the slides may fade-in/fade-out, rotate, get bigger or smaller, etc. - **[component-specific-light-dark-theme](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/component-specific-light-dark-theme.md)**: Force certain elements to be in light mode or dark mode (e.g. code blocks, media players, etc) independently of the page's color-scheme. - **[icons](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/icons.md)**: Display and manage icons that can be set and parameterized from CSS, are fast to load, crisp at any resolution and are properly exposed to (or hidden from) assistive technologies. - **[position-aware-tooltips](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/position-aware-tooltips.md)**: Build tooltips and popovers with directional arrows (or other visual styling) that automatically point the correct way when the element flips to a fallback position. - **[pull-to-reveal](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/pull-to-reveal.md)**: Build a pull-to-reveal feature that would enable the user to pull down on the screen to reveal more content, like a search bar. - **[responsive-table](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/responsive-table.md)**: Build a data table that presents tabular data with proper header semantics, and remains readable and navigable on small screens and with assistive technologies. - **[scroll-position-aware-elements](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/scroll-position-aware-elements.md)**: Build floating buttons or widgets (back-to-top, scroll-to-bottom, chat launchers, etc.) that appear and disappear based on whether the user has scrolled at all. - **[scroll-progress-indicator](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/scroll-progress-indicator.md)**: Create a scroll progress bar, stepped progress tracker, or any visual affordance that communicates how far through a page or section the user has scrolled. - **[scrollability-affordance-hints](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/scrollability-affordance-hints.md)**: Build scroll shadows or fading edges that appear only when there's actually more content to scroll to in that direction. - **[shrinking-header-on-scroll](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/shrinking-header-on-scroll.md)**: Smoothly animate a fixed header or full-page cover on scroll to dynamically shrink, gain shadows, and transform its layout over a predefined scroll distance. - **[single-line-overflow](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/single-line-overflow.md)**: Show text that must stay on one line, such as a tab label, table cell, navigation item, or file name, in a space it may not fit, without breaking the layout or losing the text. - **[state-aware-sticky-headers](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/state-aware-sticky-headers.md)**: Build sticky section headers or navbars that visually transform when they're actually "stuck" at the top, changing their color scheme or gaining a shadow. - **[viewport-aware-dropdowns](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-atoms/viewport-aware-dropdowns.md)**: Position dropdowns, flyouts, or contextual action panels tethered to a trigger button so they automatically flip axes at viewport edges instead of getting clipped.

ui-behaviors

- **[2d-panning](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/2d-panning.md)**: Allow users to freely pan or scroll two-dimensional surfaces—such as maps, zoomed images, infinite canvases, or large data grids—across both directions (whether diagonally or changing direction mid-gesture) without the gesture locking to a single horizontal or vertical axis. - **[anchor-positioning-tab-underline](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/anchor-positioning-tab-underline.md)**: Transition an element seamlessly between two target element positions. For example, moving a selected tab underline between the previously selected tab and the currently selected tab. - **[animate-element-entry-exit](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/animate-element-entry-exit.md)**: Smoothly hide/show elements as they are added/removed from the DOM or as their display values are toggled. - **[animate-to-from-top-layer](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/animate-to-from-top-layer.md)**: Animate elements such as dialogs, popovers, and tooltips as they're entering/exiting the top layer. - **[carousel-snap-highlights](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/carousel-snap-highlights.md)**: Visually highlight the currently snapped non-interactive item in scroll-snapping carousels, galleries, or full-page swipe experiences. For example, expanding a card when snapped, or revealing hidden content. - **[consistent-cross-document-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/consistent-cross-document-transitions.md)**: Ensure critical page state is loaded and stable before initiating a cross-document view transition. This means critical CSS styles are loaded and applied, critical JavaScript is loaded and run, and the HTML visible for the user's initial view of the page has been parsed before the transition runs. - **[cross-document-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/cross-document-transitions.md)**: Create smooth, seamless transitions between full page navigations, such as cross-fades, custom reveal effects, or morphing of content from one page to the next. - **[custom-button-actions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/custom-button-actions.md)**: Declaratively connect a button to any element to trigger custom, application-specific actions using declarative button commands, invoker commands, button commands, custom commands, or declarative toggle actions. - **[declarative-dialog-popover-control](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/declarative-dialog-popover-control.md)**: Toggle the visibility of a dialog or popover from a button without writing JavaScript. - **[directional-navigation-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/directional-navigation-transitions.md)**: Animate visual state changes to reflect the direction of a user's navigational flow, such as sliding new content in from the right when advancing forward or from the left when returning to a previous screen. - **[drag](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/drag.md)**: Support dragging to move a floating element around the page. - **[drag-and-drop](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/drag-and-drop.md)**: Support dragging to rearrange the children of a container along one axis (horizontal or vertical) while preserving their state and accessible order. - **[dynamic-sibling-animations](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/dynamic-sibling-animations.md)**: Stagger animation or transition timing across sibling elements so each one starts after a computed delay based on its position in the sibling list. - **[dynamic-sort](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/dynamic-sort.md)**: Best practices for handling dynamic user-triggered reordering of a container's children (e.g. list items, table rows, or a card grid), with optional animated reordering that respects user preferences, good screen reader UX, and optimal performance for large lists. - **[group-element-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/group-element-transitions.md)**: Smoothly rearrange and animate list items, cards, or grid elements into their new positions simultaneously when adding, removing, shuffling, or reordering—such as removing a product from a shopping cart. - **[highlight-text-ranges](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/highlight-text-ranges.md)**: Highlight arbitrary text ranges on a page such as search results, spelling errors, or collaborative editing cursors. - **[interactive-content-reveal](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/interactive-content-reveal.md)**: Create interactive reveal effects, such as a spotlight that follows the user's pointer to uncover details within an image or UI section. - **[interest-triggered-action-previews](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/interest-triggered-action-previews.md)**: Show a live preview of a button's effect when a user signals interest (e.g. hovering, focusing, or long-pressing) but before they commit to clicking. - **[interest-triggered-tooltips](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/interest-triggered-tooltips.md)**: Show a tooltip or supplemental information when a user hovers over, focuses on, or long-presses an interactive element, without requiring a click. - **[light-dismiss-a-dialog](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/light-dismiss-a-dialog.md)**: Create a modal dialog that can be closed via light dismiss (i.e. clicking or tapping outside of the dialog) - **[motion](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/motion.md)**: Animate UI with CSS transitions, animations, scroll-driven animations, and view transitions while keeping motion on the compositor and respecting reduced-motion preferences. - **[move-dom-element-without-losing-state](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/move-dom-element-without-losing-state.md)**: Move or reparent a DOM element without losing important element state, such as interactivity states (:focus/:active), `<iframe>` loading state, animation/transition state, etc - **[parallax-scroll-effects](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/parallax-scroll-effects.md)**: Create scroll-based effects (such as parallax) where foreground and background layers move at different rates, creating a sense of depth as the user scrolls. - **[persistent-top-layer-ui](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/persistent-top-layer-ui.md)**: Keep a modal dialog, fullscreen element, or native popover visibly open and functionally active when its underlying DOM node is moved or reparented in the DOM. - **[physics-based-easing](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/physics-based-easing.md)**: Create custom, physics-based animation and transition effects, like bounce and spring, that feel more natural and engaging than traditional easing curves. - **[platform-controls-dismiss-dialog](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/platform-controls-dismiss-dialog.md)**: Create a modal dialog that can be closed via standard platform-specific user actions, such as pressing the `Esc` key on desktop platforms, or a "back" or "dismiss" gesture on mobile platforms - **[prevent-page-scroll-under-modal-dialog](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/prevent-page-scroll-under-modal-dialog.md)**: Prevent the underlying page from scrolling while a modal dialog is open. - **[same-document-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/same-document-transitions.md)**: Visually connect persisting elements across different page states or navigations in a Single Page Application (SPA) (e.g. expanding a product thumbnail into a full-bleed hero image) by smoothly morphing their size, position, or other styling properties. - **[scoped-component-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/scoped-component-transitions.md)**: Animate state changes inside a single component (a card, list, panel, or other subtree) while the rest of the page remains interactive, and other transitions run concurrently. - **[scroll-completion-effects](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/scroll-completion-effects.md)**: Trigger visual effects,

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible system `ps` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/getting-started/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup records the selected runtime and REA entry script directly. If acquired through a package runner, keep its cache entry available. Run package acquisition from a trusted directory outside the target project. Installation and recovery details are in the setup guide below. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/getting-started/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md) for provider configuration, manual MCP registration, Claude Code/Codex plugins, and the Cursor Marketplace plugin. MCP advertises compact input schemas to reduce context overhead; guidance a compact schema omits follows the tool description. The full tool set and canonical server validation are unchanged. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. Output schemas are omitted from `tools/list` by default: no model API reads them, and REA validates every result itself. Set `REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact` to advertise each output schema within a 4,096-byte budget. Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/getting-started/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` `rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. ![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg) [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm. Additional tools and host support depend on the target: | Target | What REA returns | Requirements and guide | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Desktop installations | Runtime candidates, supporting files, component markers and next probes | Built-in bounded directory/header inspection; [desktop applications](docs/desktop-applications.md) | | Native binaries | Pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls and references | Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna; [native analysis](docs/guides/native/native-investigation.md) | | Offline ELF layout | Sections, segments, original symbols/relocations and static mitigation candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; [binary diagnostics](docs/guides/native/binary-diagnostics.md) | | Go binaries | Embedded compiler version, modules, replacements and build settings | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; no Go installation required | | GPU code objects | CUDA/HIP targets, selected kernel parameters and resources, retained PTX text | Built-in static ELF/PE/fatbin/CUBIN/PTX inspection; [GPU code objects](docs/gpu-code-objects.md) | | Model artifacts | GGUF / safetensors metadata, tensor declarations and derived totals | Built-in header inspection; optional full-file hash; [model files](docs/model-artifacts.md) | | IL2CPP metadata | Unity global-metadata.dat assembly images, type and method names and index ranges | Built-in static decoding of versions 24, 27, 29, 31 and 39; no Unity required | | Godot PCK | Archive inventory and extraction, original header/directory facts and selected content identities | Built-in static formats 2, 3 and 4; no Godot required | | Rust binaries | Embedded cargo-auditable crate names, versions, sources and dependency edges | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; [Rust binaries](docs/rust-binaries.md) | | PE certificates | Authenticode WIN_CERTIFICATE entries and PKCS#7 signer/X.509 identity fields | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE certificates](docs/pe-certificates.md) | | PE imports | Import and delay-load DLL names, ordinals, IAT RVAs and pefile import hash | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE imports](docs/pe-imports.md) | | Windows shortcuts | Shell Link target, arguments, working dir, ExtraData and Tracker droid facts | Built-in static LNK inspection; [Windows shortcuts](docs/guides/native/windows-shortcut.md) | | ELF notes | PT_NOTE/SHT_NOTE owners, types, GNU build-id and ABI-tag fields | Built-in static ELF inspection; [ELF notes](docs/elf-notes.md) | | DWARF compile units | Compile-unit name, directory, producer, language, and dwo_name | Built-in static ELF, Mach-O, and PE inspection; [DWARF compile units](docs/guides/native/dwarf-units.md) | | ELF dependencies | DT_NEEDED, SONAME, RPATH/RUNPATH, GNU versions, and undefined imports | Built-in static ELF inspection; [ELF dependencies](docs/elf-dependencies.md) | | Binary hardening | PIE, NX, RELRO, CFG and related header flags for ELF, PE and Mach-O | Built-in static header inspection; [binary hardening](docs/binary-hardening.md) | | Apple IPS crashes | .ips metadata, threads, images, registers and documented crash classes | Built-in static JSON inspection; [Apple IPS](docs/apple-ips.md) | | Linux kernel modules | .modinfo keys, __versions CRCs, this_module presence, and signature trailer | Built-in static ELF inspection; [kernel modules](docs/kernel-modules.md) | | Erlang BEAM | IFF chunks, atoms, exports, imports, lambdas and the Code header | Built-in static BEAM inspection; [Erlang BEAM](docs/erlang-beam.md) | | NuGet packages | Package identity, dependency groups, license, repository and ZIP contents | Built-in static .nupkg inspection; [NuGet packages](docs/guides/managed/nuget-nupkg.md) | | WASM artifact | Validation, sections, exact import/export WAT forms and decoded WAT | Caller-supplied WABT 1.0.42; `inspect_wasm_artifact` | | EVM bytecode | Dispatch selectors, byte offsets, inferred arguments and mutability | Local raw/hex carrier on Linux x64; [offline EVM guide](docs/guides/evm/evm-bytecode.md) | | SQLite databases | Tables, columns, indexes, views, triggers and selected ordinary-table rows | Local database/WAL snapshot; Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ with native SQLite limits | | Recorded Linux crashes | Raw notes, every recorded thread's registers/signals and optional mapping candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; optional GDB/pwndbg; [recorded crashes](docs/guides/native/recorded-crashes.md) | | JavaScript / Electron | Modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC, native add-ons, `rea audit-release-exposure` | Node.js and npm; Linux: procps-compatible `ps`; [application analysis](docs/guides/javascript/javascript-application-workflows.md) | | Websites | Page structure, scripts, network observations and requested screenshots | A Chrome-family browser; [browser analysis](docs/guides/web/browser-observation.md) | | Saved network captures | Requests, responses, exposed payloads and source locations | HAR or Fiddler Everywhere SAZ; mitmdump on Linux for native mitmproxy; [capture guide](docs/guides/web/web-network-captures.md) | | .NET assemblies | Metadata, CIL instructions, declared native dependencies and build comparisons | None (static only); [managed-code guide](docs/guides/managed/managed-code-analysis.md) | | Android APKs | Manifest declarations, classes, decompiled methods and references | Headless JADX and a full JDK on Linux/macOS/Windows x64; [Android guide](docs/guides/android/android-analysis.md) | | APK signatures | v1/v2/v3/v3.1 signers, certificate fingerprints, key rotation and digest self-consistency | None (static only); `inspect_apk_signature` | | Android devices | Devices, packages, processes, logs, dumps, screen captures, and APK/file transfers | Caller-supplied adb (emulator or hardware); [ADB guide](docs/guides/android/adb-device-analysis.md) | | JEB projects | Engine-backed project units, artifact digests and type/method pseudo-code | A caller-started JEB client serving MCP, selected with REA_JEB_MCP_URL; [JEB guide](docs/providers/jeb-analysis.md) | | Android resources | Decoded manifest, string tables, locales and version facts | Caller-supplied Apktool launcher; [resource guide](docs/guides/android/apktool-resource-analysis.md) | | Flutter apps | Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance | None (static APK parsing); [Flutter guide](docs/guides/android/flutter-analysis.md) | | Firmware | Regions, extraction results and native-analysis handoffs | Binwalk / Unblob on Linux; [firmware guide](docs/guides/firmware/firmware-analysis.md) | | Recorded packets | Selected fields, repeated values, filters and decode-as rules | Linux: TShark 4.x + prlimit; [capture guide](docs/guides/data/packet-captures.md) | | Packet summaries | Endpoints, DNS, TLS SNI, protocol distribution and HTTP requests | Caller-supplied tshark and capinfos (Linux-verified); [pcap guide](docs/guides/data/pcap-analysis.md) | | Recorded logic signals | Decoder annotations, sample ranges and diagnostics | Linux: sigrok-cli 0.7.2 + prlimit; [signal recordings](docs/guides/signals/signal-recordings.md) | | Packages and resources | File inventories, digests, plists, Apple bundle anatomy and extracted resources | [Artifact and JavaScript guide](docs/guides/javascript/javascript-artifact-reconstruction.md), [Apple applications](docs/guides/apple/apple-application-analysis.md) | | Process behavior | Terminal output, interactions, exit and filesystem observations, and run comparisons | Linux/macOS with a native PTY; [process capture](docs/guides/runtime/process-capture.md) | | PyInstaller executables | CArchive members, Python version, entry scripts and extracted bytecode | None (static only); [Python packaged applications](docs/python-packaged-applications.md) | | Deno compile binaries | Virtual files, entry point, recorded options, npm snapshot length | None (static only); [Deno compile executables](docs/deno-standalone.md) | Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects. For offline native-binary inspection, REA also supports caller-supplied GNU objdump and Rizin. See the [reverse-engineering tools guide](docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md) for provider setup, CLI commands, and Evidence limitations. REA does not install or update either provider. Native formats and host support vary by provider. See [Hopper and Ghidra setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md#hopper), the [IDA guide](docs/providers/ida-provider.md) (including an optional native MCP bridge), the [Kuna decompiler guide](docs/kuna-provider.md), and [experimental Windows Ghidra support](docs/providers/windows-ghidra-p0.md). Ghidra also supports [16-bit DOS analysis](docs/providers/ghidra-dos.md). For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with `REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS` or `REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS`. For provider selection, see the [CLI guide](docs/getting-started/cli.md#choose-a-provider). Check [release availability](docs/getting-started/installation.md#released-package-and-main) for features added since the latest npm release. ## Showcases ### DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation Follow a sound call into its position-to-pan helper, inspect the instructions, and turn incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passes 3,205 original-x86 cases and reproduces all 63 compiled function bytes. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/dx-ball/) · [Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/dx-ball) ### Notion: trace the Electron clipboard bridge Find the renderer's clipboard API, follow it through preload and IPC into the main process, and inspect the rich clipboard format. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/notion/) ### TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring calculation Inspect the original PC-98 game's 16-bit instructions, recover the fixed and aimed angle calculations, and compare the reconstructed C++ with the historical compiler output. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/th04/) · [Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04) ### Build RL environments with REA Record a web app session, turn its API into tools, and export an environment an AI agent can use. Run it with AgentEnv, then add tasks and reward checks for RL training or evaluation. [Read the guide](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/) · [Watch the video](https://x.com/reatools/status/2112574822584918075?s=20) If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your case in an [issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) or a [pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls), including the target, your question, how REA helped, and what you found. ## Build RL environments Give an AI agent a local environment to practice tasks such as finding an issue or creating a folder, without running the original app. Use it for reinforcement learning (RL) or to test how well an agent completes tasks. REA turns recorded API requests and responses into tools the agent can call. The environment uses the recorded data and supports changes only when the recording confirms their effects. With REA set up in your agent, replace the example URL and folder tasks below with your own: ```text Use REA to build an RL environment from my test web app at http://127.0.0.1:3000. Cover listing, creating, renaming, and deleting folders. You may create and remove test folders. Leave existing data unchanged. Save it in a folder named my-env. Check which operations work and tell me how to run it. ```
Use the command line instead Use these commands if you already have a file containing the app’s recorded browser requests and responses. Running the result also requires AgentEnv and Docker. ```sh rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json agent-env run ./my-env ```
REA exports a runnable environment with a basic test to check that it starts and responds. Use it with your RL framework to define task goals, add reward checks, and run training. [Build an environment](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/) · [Environment reference](docs/agent-environments.md) · [Watch the demo on X](https://x.com/reatools/status/2112574822584918075?s=20) ### Desktop app environments REA can also build an environment of a Linux desktop app, which an agent uses through screenshots, the mouse and the keyboard. From a one-line request, such as "Build me a Gnote environment where the agent adds olive oil to the shopping list note", your agent installs the app on a local build computer, writes the task, exports the environment and checks the task in a fresh computer. The machine that builds it needs Linux on amd64 or arm64, Docker and the agentenv framework version the guide pins. [Set up desktop app environments](docs/desktop-build-computer.md) ## FAQ
Which agents can use REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the [supported agents](docs/getting-started/installation.md#supported-agents); other clients can use [manual MCP registration](docs/getting-started/installation.md#mcp-registry).
Do I need a native analysis engine? Deep native analysis uses Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna, depending on the target and operation. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra, IDA and Kuna use your existing installations. See [provider setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md#hopper) for the options and their supported targets.
Do I need to start Hopper first? REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See [Hopper startup and troubleshooting](docs/getting-started/installation.md#launcher-paths-and-troubleshooting).
What does installing the skill from skills.sh do? The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use `npx rea-agents setup` to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See [skill-only installation](docs/getting-started/installation.md#skill-only-installation).
What code does REA return? Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the [showcases](#showcases) give worked examples.
Does REA upload my app? REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy.
What should I do if I hit a bug? Update first; a recent release may already fix it. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` For agent setup through `npx`: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` If you're using an agent, complete the [setup refresh](#update-rea) and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.
## Documentation Start with the website's [worked guides](https://rea.tools/guides/). For exact options, prerequisites and result contracts: - [Installation and setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md): agent registration, provider configuration, updates and uninstall. - [Readiness and troubleshooting](docs/getting-started/installation.md#check-readiness-for-your-task): diagnose one agent or analysis engine. - [CLI and Evidence](docs/getting-started/cli.md): commands, provider selection, snapshots, import/export and exit statuses. - [MCP contracts](docs/reference/mcp-contracts.md) and [agent prompts](docs/getting-started/mcp-prompts.md): tool results, sessions and guided investigations. - [Tool catalog](docs/reference/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog): generated inventory of tools, providers and CLI commands. - [Roadmap](docs/development/roadmap.md): planned work and capability trackers. Report vulnerabilities through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Star history 🎉 **400,000 GitHub stars — thank you!** Thanks to everyone using REA, reporting bugs, requesting features, testing builds, and contributing fixes. ## Disclaimer See [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md) for responsible-use guidance. The project's position on illegal or unauthorized use covers all REA versions, distribution channels, and platforms; each copy retains its applicable licenses. REA is for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you own or are authorized to examine. ## Contributing We'd love your help with REA! [Open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) to report a bug or suggest a feature, or [send a pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls) to improve the code or docs. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup and checks, [testing](docs/development/testing.md) for verification lanes, and the [architecture map](docs/architecture/architecture.mermaid) for selected layers and dependency paths. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) REA-authored code is licensed under MIT. Third-party material retains its own licenses and copyright notices; see [Third-party notices](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) for the dependency inventory, preserved license texts, and external-tool terms. **You must legally obtain and be authorized to use commercial tools**, including IDA Pro / Hex-Rays decompilers, Hopper, and JEB, under their applicable licenses. REA grants no tool license, key, or activation entitlement. Trials and demos remain subject to vendor terms, including user, feature, automation, and output sharing restrictions. Cracked copies, stolen keys, unauthorized key sharing, and bypassing license restrictions are not authorized. This guidance does not amend MIT or third-party licenses.

items.readme_text:
An e-signature app for your own organization, on your own Vercel account.
Upload a PDF, place fields, send signing links, and keep the sealed, signed copy with its audit certificate.


or copy this to your LLM

Features · SignuDoc vs DocuSign · What it costs · Get started · Self-hosting guide

## Why SignuDoc **No seats to pay for.** SignuDoc is open source, and the Deploy button sets it up on free plans from Vercel, Neon and Resend, which carry about 250 documents a month for $0. A 15-person team pays DocuSign $8,100 a year for Business Pro seats, or $5,400 for Standard. SignuDoc costs the same whether one person sends or fifty. **No envelope allowance to watch.** DocuSign's Standard and Business Pro plans include 100 envelopes per user per year. SignuDoc has no limit of its own. What you can send depends on your hosting plans, and the free ones carry about 250 documents a month. **Your documents stay in your accounts.** PDFs live in a private Vercel Blob store and everything else in a Neon Postgres database, both in your name and in the region you choose. Nobody else hosts your agreements, and the code is yours to read, change and run. **Evidence anyone can check.** Every finished PDF and its audit certificate carry a PAdES seal that PDF readers check for changes, the audit trail is hash-chained so an edited or deleted row shows, and anyone holding a copy can check it on the install's public Verify page. **One click, nothing to look after.** The Deploy button creates the database, the file store and email for you, on free plans. There are no servers to patch, and every push to your copy deploys again. ## Everything it takes to get a document signed

### Prepare a document in minutes Upload a PDF, add up to 10 signers in the order they sign, and add people who only receive the finished copy. Then place fields where they belong: signature, initials, date, name, text, number, checkbox, dropdown and radio buttons, each required or optional and each tied to one signer. ![Placing signature, date and dropdown fields for two signers on a master services agreement](docs/images/prepare.png)

The organization, people and documents in these screenshots are made up.

### Signing without an account Each signer gets a link by email, agrees to use electronic records, and signs with a typed or drawn signature on any phone, tablet or computer. Fields from earlier signers stay visible and locked. Signers can download the document before they sign, or decline with a reason, and the sender is told. ![Jordan Lee signing a consulting agreement with a drawn signature, with the earlier signer's signature locked](docs/images/signing.png) ### Know who is signing For documents that need more than an email link, ask a signer for an access code you give them yourself, or have SignuDoc email a one-time code when they open the link. The audit certificate records how each signer was checked, with their IP address and browser. ### Follow every envelope The dashboard shows each document as a card with its first page, its status (draft, sent, completed, declined, voided or expired) and who it waits on, with search and a status filter. Each envelope has its own signing deadline, from 3 to 90 days, which you can change while it is out, and automatic reminders every 1, 2, 3 or 7 days, on top of the reminder you can send by hand. ![The dashboard: six documents as cards, with drafts, a sent offer letter, an NDA one of two signed, and completed agreements](docs/images/dashboard.png) ![A sent NDA: its deadline, reminders and Save as template, the two signers, and the timeline](docs/images/envelope.png) ### Templates for the documents you send every week Open any envelope and choose Save as template. The template keeps the document, the fields and the signing order, with roles instead of names. Using it asks who signs this time and opens a draft ready to send. ### Sealed, certified, and checkable by anyone When the last signer finishes, SignuDoc builds the signed PDF and an audit certificate, seals both, and emails them to every signer and copy recipient. Names and text in Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Chinese, Japanese and Korean scripts are drawn correctly. Anyone can drop a copy on the Verify page to see whether it is exactly the file the site produced; the file never leaves their device, only its fingerprint does. ![The Verify page confirming that a signed contractor agreement is unchanged](docs/images/verify.png) ### Your name, logo and color Signers see your organization, not SignuDoc. Give the install your name, logo and brand color, and they appear on the site, the signing pages and every email. Serve it at your own domain and link your own terms and privacy policy. ![The same signing page in the organization's own green, with its logo](docs/images/branding.png) ### Run by your administrators The first account is the administrator, and you can make more. Choose who may create an account: people at your email domains, nobody, or anyone. People who only sign never need one. Set how long finished documents are kept, and answer a signer who asks for their data with a built-in export or erasure tool. ### On your phone SignuDoc works on small screens as well as large ones: check on your documents from your phone, and signers sign from theirs.

## SignuDoc and DocuSign, side by side DocuSign does more, and charges for it per user. SignuDoc does the everyday signing loop well, and it's yours. DocuSign's plans are as [DocuSign listed them](https://ecom.docusign.com/plans-and-pricing/esignature) in November 2026, for the US.

### Price and ownership | | SignuDoc | DocuSign eSignature | | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Price** | Free and open source, on free plans from Vercel, Neon and Resend | $11 (Personal), $30 (Standard) or $45 (Business Pro) per user a month, on an annual plan | | **Envelopes** | No limit of its own. The free plans carry about 250 a month | 5 a month on Personal, 100 per user a year on Standard and Business Pro | | **Where it runs** | Your Vercel account, with your Neon database and Blob store | DocuSign's cloud | | **Where data is kept** | The region you choose, the EU included | DocuSign's data centers, the EU included | | **Source code** | MIT license, on GitHub | Closed | | **Your own domain and branding** | ✅ your domain, logo and color, in every install | Logo and colors from Standard | ### The signing loop | | SignuDoc | DocuSign eSignature | | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Signing without an account** | ✅ | ✅ | | **Signing order** | ✅ in order, up to 10 signers | ✅ in order, at the same time, or mixed | | **People who only get a copy** | ✅ | ✅ and more roles: approvers, editors, in-person signers | | **Field types** | ✅ signature, initials, date, name, text, number, checkbox, dropdown, radio, each required or optional | ✅ more types; It copies SignuDoc into your GitHub account and builds your site from that copy. 2. **Add the three things Vercel offers to create**, each on a free plan: [Resend](https://resend.com) for email, a [Neon](https://neon.com) Postgres database, and a private [Vercel Blob](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob) store. 3. **Click Deploy.** The build creates the database tables by itself. If Vercel stops with "One or more integration resources failed to provision", nothing is wrong with your copy: Resend was still checking its domain. Wait a minute or two, refresh the page, and click **Redeploy**. See [If the first deployment fails](docs/self-hosting.md#if-the-first-deployment-fails). 4. **Open your new site.** Name your organization, give the email address people should write to for help, and create the first account, which is the administrator. 5. **Set up the address you send from.** Under Settings, Organization, enter an address at your own domain. The site lists the DNS records to add and checks them for you. **Taking new versions.** Settings, SignuDoc, **Check for updates** tells you when a new release is out and what is in it. A workflow that comes with your copy then opens a pull request with the release in your GitHub repository; merge it and Vercel deploys the update. See [Keep your install up to date](docs/self-hosting.md#keep-your-install-up-to-date). **Deploying with an AI agent.** An agent that can use your browser can do all of this for you. Point it at [docs/deploy-with-an-agent.md](docs/deploy-with-an-agent.md), which lists every screen, what to choose, what to ask you, and how to retry. There is nothing to type in Vercel and no terminal to open. Until step 5 is done, email reaches only the address on your Resend account, so you can try the whole product straight away by sending a document to yourself. The [self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md) covers your own domain, locking down a new install, keeping it up to date, running in the EU, and every optional setting. ### Try it on your computer With Node.js 24 and Docker: ```bash npm install cp .env.example .env npm run db:start # Postgres in Docker, with the schema applied npm run dev # SignuDoc at http://localhost:3000 ``` Files stay on disk and emails are written to `.data/outbox` instead of being sent, so you need no outside account. [Development](docs/development.md) says more. ## Built on Vercel - **Vercel-native from end to end.** Next.js 16 on Vercel Functions, Neon Postgres and Resend from the Vercel Marketplace, private Vercel Blob storage with direct browser uploads, a daily Vercel cron job for reminders and cleanup, and optional [Vercel BotID](https://vercel.com/docs/botid). - **Secure by default.** Private file storage with no public URLs, a strict Content Security Policy, rate limits kept in Postgres, signing links that are hashed at rest, and a setup page that only the first visitor, or the holder of a `SETUP_TOKEN`, can use. - **Tested.** Unit tests, database tests against a real Postgres, and a browser test that sets up a fresh install, sends a document and signs it, run on every pull request. ## Using SignuDoc for real agreements SignuDoc is not a law firm and does not give legal advice, and nothing here is a promise that a signature made with it will be accepted for a given purpose. It gives you the features that electronic signature laws such as the US ESIGN Act and UETA and the EU's eIDAS regulation look for in a simple electronic signature: each signer's consent to electronic records, a record of who signed, when and how, optional identity checks, and a sealed copy that shows any change. Whether that is enough for a particular document depends on the document, where you and the signers are, and how you use it. Ask a lawyer when it matters. Every install has a page at `/electronic-signatures` that says what it is for, and senders confirm it before each send. It is meant for ordinary business agreements, such as contracts, NDAs, statements of work, offer letters, purchase orders and approvals. It is **not** built for: - documents that need an advanced or qualified electronic signature (AdES or QES) under eIDAS, unless you add a signing provider (see below); - protected health information under HIPAA; - documents that many laws keep out of electronic signature, such as wills, family-law matters, court orders, notices of foreclosure, eviction, utility shut-off or insurance cancellation, and in most EU countries real estate transfers and documents that need a notary. For **advanced or qualified electronic signatures** under eIDAS, connect a signing provider: [eID Easy](https://eideasy.com), or a trust service provider's remote signing service that speaks the CSC API v2. A sender can then choose that signature type for an envelope, and each signer proves who they are at the provider and signs with a certificate in their own name. Every signature goes into the PDF in a revision of its own, so all of them stay valid, and the finished PDF gets long-term validation. The provider is a paid service outside Vercel, so it is optional, and the flow has been tested against stand-ins for both interfaces but not yet against the live services. [Signatures in the signers' own names](docs/self-hosting.md#signatures-in-the-signers-own-names-eidas-ades-and-qes) has the setup. For FDA 21 CFR Part 11 records, an administrator can turn on **Part 11 mode** under Settings. Signers then sign with their own accounts, whose identity an administrator has confirmed, give their password again at each signature, and see the meaning of their signature (approval, review, responsibility or authorship) printed beside it with their name and the time. Audit trails export as CSV, and finished records are never deleted on a timer. That covers the software's part only: validating your install, writing and following your own procedures, training your people and certifying your electronic signatures to the FDA stay with your organization. The [Part 11 validation pack](docs/part11/README.md) gives you starting documents for that: requirements, a traceability matrix, a risk assessment, qualification scripts, SOP templates and the FDA letter. Your install carries your organization's name, and your organization is responsible for how it is used: linking your own terms and privacy policy, keeping the support address pointed at a mailbox someone reads, choosing how long documents are kept, and answering signers' data requests. [Your responsibilities](docs/self-hosting.md#your-responsibilities) has the details. ## Learn more - [Self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md): deploying, first-run setup, what it costs, your own domain, updates, the EU, the seal, cleanup, rate limits, bot protection and every optional setting. - [Development](docs/development.md): running SignuDoc locally, storage, the database, email, tests and the code's layout. - [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Security](SECURITY.md). ## License and credits SignuDoc is [MIT licensed](LICENSE). #
🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing
Yiwen Song1, Yale Song1, Tomas Pfister1, and Jinsung Yoon1
1Google Cloud AI Research


PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers.
## Key Features - **Multi-Agent Pipeline**: Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. - **Comprehensive Literature Synthesis**: Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. - **Visuals Generation**: Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. - **LaTeX Automation**: Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. ## Installation 1. **Environment Setup**: The project relies on a Conda environment named `paper_orchestra`. You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies. ```bash conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11 conda activate paper_orchestra pip install -r requirements.txt ``` 2. **Environment Variables**: Create a `.env` file in the root of the project and add your API keys: ```env # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty # You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model # For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY # If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY=your_semantic_scholar_api_key OPENAI_API_KEY=your_openai_api_key VERTEX_AI_PROJECT=your_vertex_ai_project VERTEX_AI_LOCATION=your_vertex_ai_location GEMINI_API_KEY=your_gemini_api_key # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well SMTP_EMAIL=your_email SMTP_PASSWORD=your_password ``` ## Dataset The dataset used for paper generation is **not included** in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date. Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the `datasets/` directory. ## Usage You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI. ### Using the Bash Script ```bash ./paper_writing_cli.sh ``` ### Using the Python CLI directly ```bash python paper_writing_cli.py \ --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \ --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \ --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \ --use_plotting true ``` ### Key Arguments * `--raw_materials_dir`: (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log). * `--latex_template_dir`: (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., `templates/cvpr2025`). * `--output_dir`: Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created. * `--use_plotting`: Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: `False`). * `--writer_model_name`: LLM for writer and literature agents. * `--reflection_model_name`: LLM for reflection agents. ### Interactive Demo We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the [README.md](frontend/README.md) in the `frontend` directory. ## Project Structure * `autoraters/`: Contains scripts for automated evaluation. * `methods/`: Core logic for agents and pipeline execution. * `templates/`: LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory. * `utils/`: Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc. ## Citation If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows: ```bibtex @article{song2026paperorchestra, title={PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing}, author={Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018}, year={2026} } ``` # Disclaimer This is not an officially supported Google product.
